strapline: Fuel up again for November, a Mandevu seat decided without a vote, a Tier B world title in Baku, and Munali Suns unbeaten in Lusaka

stories.title: Petrol K33.06, diesel K34.45: the ERB raises every fuel price for November on a weaker kwacha and Gulf tensions, a day after Nalumango ruled out using reserves at the pump
stories.excerpt: A month after the K6 jump that followed the end of the tax relief, the Energy Regulation Board has added K1.60 to petrol and K1.18 to diesel from midnight on Saturday 31 October. Kerosene goes to K32.08 and Jet A-1 to K34.51. The board says international prices rose for petrol and kerosene and the kwacha lost more than 3 per cent; diesel went up even though its international price fell. On Friday Mutale Nalumango told Parliament the country's US$6.5 billion in reserves would not be used for fuel.

image.label: November at the pump
image.caption: The Energy Regulation Board's November 2026 price review, announced on Saturday 31 October, raised petrol to K33.06 and diesel to K34.45 a litre.

body: The second rise in as many months arrived on a Saturday. In a statement issued on 31 October, the Energy Regulation Board said that from midnight the pump price of petrol would be K33.06 a litre, up K1.60 from K31.46, and diesel K34.45, up K1.18 from K33.27. News Diggers and the Zambian Observer both carried the figures; Zambia Monitor reported the same diesel price and put kerosene at K32.08 and Jet A-1 at K34.51. The board's October statement, still on its website, listed kerosene at K29.76 and Jet A-1 at K31.85, so both have risen by more than K2.

The reasons given by ERB board chairperson James Banda were the usual two. International oil prices, he said, trended upward through the review period on what the board called sustained geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, and the kwacha weakened against the US dollar, depreciating by more than 3 per cent. The combined effect, the statement said, was the main factor in the November prices. The Zambian Observer and Zambia Monitor reproduced the board's benchmark figures: the average international price of petrol rose to US$125.84 a barrel from US$121.58, and kerosene and Jet A-1 to US$153.22 from US$144.00. Diesel, by contrast, fell to US$154.71 from US$160.88, which means the diesel increase at the pump rests on the exchange rate alone. None of the reports gave the exchange rate the board used.

body.text: The October step, and the one still to come

body: November's increase is modest beside October's. The board's statement of 30 September, still published on the ERB website, raised petrol by K6.17 and diesel by K6.41 in a single review, because the government's tax relief on fuel expired in September and excise duty returned from 1 October. That statement put the kwacha at K19.76 to the dollar, from K19.28 the month before, a fall of about 2.5 per cent. It also recorded a date that has not changed: the zero-rating of VAT on fuel ends on 1 December 2026. If nothing else moves, the December review will have to absorb that too.

The new prices came a day after the Vice-President was asked in Parliament whether the Treasury could do something about them. During Friday's Vice-President's Question Time, Getrude Imenda asked whether part of the country's reserves could be used to cushion fuel. Mutale Nalumango said no. The reserves, which she put at US$6.5 billion, were a national security resource that should not be used carelessly, she said; the government had already given up duty revenue on fuel, which amounted to the same thing, and the budget, through free education, social cash transfers, farm inputs and cash-for-work, was where the cost of living was addressed. Kalemba's account of the exchange, carried by the Zambian Observer, and News Diggers' report of the same sitting agree on the substance. She also argued that Zambia's prices compared well with the region and that neighbouring countries buy fuel here.

body.text: Fuel prices are high, we agree.
body.attribution: Mutale Nalumango, Vice-President, during the Vice-President's Question Time in the National Assembly on Friday 30 October, as reported by Kalemba and carried by the Zambian Observer

body.text: The budget takes care of the cost of living. We can't get reserves for fuel.
body.attribution: Mutale Nalumango, the same sitting, as reported by Kalemba and carried by the Zambian Observer

body: The exchange rate that drove the diesel increase is the same one the Bank of Zambia's Financial Stability Committee discussed at its October meeting. Zambia Monitor reported on Saturday that the committee kept the countercyclical capital buffer at zero but said near-term risks had risen since April, naming prolonged geopolitical tensions and the higher energy and fertiliser prices they bring, tighter global financial conditions and the El Niño drought that is expected this season. On the other side of the ledger, the committee said government securities yields had fallen, liquidity had improved and the kwacha's volatility had declined, and that banks would stay above the 10 per cent capital requirement even under a severe drought scenario. The statement itself had not appeared on the bank's website by Sunday; the account here is Zambia Monitor's.

The October increases, the September exchange rate and the 1 December VAT date are in the ERB's own October statement. The Vice-President's remarks on reserves are reported by Kalemba (via the Zambian Observer) and News Diggers.

stories.title: No ballot in Mandevu: the ECZ will declare Adrian Banda MP on 5 November, Tonse asks for a rerun with a new candidate, and Nalumango says a retreating opposition could gift 2031
stories.excerpt: The Electoral Commission's public notice of Friday 30 October ends the Mandevu contest without a vote: with the FDD's Daniel Chisenga, the Leadership Movement's Ntazana Mutungwa and the independent Daniel Daka out, the UPND's Adrian Banda is the only validly nominated candidate and will be declared elected. The Tonse Alliance wants the poll cancelled so it can field someone else. In Parliament, Mutale Nalumango mocked the withdrawals; Citizens First's Harry Kalaba said she had a point.

image.label: One name, no poll
image.caption: The ECZ's notice of Friday 30 October 2026 says Adrian Banda will be declared Member of Parliament for Mandevu on 5 November without an election, after his three rivals withdrew.

body: The Mandevu by-election will not be held. In a public notice issued on Friday 30 October, the Electoral Commission of Zambia's chief electoral officer, Brown Kasaro, said the commission had received letters of withdrawal dated 28 October from Daniel Chisenga of the Forum for Democracy and Development, Ntazana Musukuma Mutungwa of the Leadership Movement and the independent Daniel Daka, and that under Regulations 20(3) and 52(2) of the Electoral Process (General) Regulations of 2016 the remaining candidate, the UPND's Adrian Banda, would be declared elected with effect from 5 November, the day the poll had been set for. Zambia Monitor and the Times of Zambia both reported the notice; the Times said the letters reached the commission on 29 October and took immediate effect.

body.text: will be declared duly elected Member of Parliament of Mandevu Constituency without the need for an election
body.attribution: Brown Kasaro, Chief Electoral Officer, in the ECZ's public notice of Friday 30 October, as quoted by Zambia Monitor

body: The notice gave no reasons for the withdrawals and did not say whether the commission had received any complaint about intimidation, Zambia Monitor noted, although the withdrawals followed reported allegations of threats against opposition candidates during the campaign. The Times of Zambia put the result in the context of the House: by its count the UPND now holds 161 seats against 84 for the combined opposition and 20 independents. It also recorded that Mandevu was not the only walkover of the round. In Lumezi North the UPND's Anderson Banda was unopposed after the Leadership Movement's Nebby Manda withdrew, and in the Mbala mayoral race the UPND's Felix Mulwanda was left alone when the Progressive Alliance Party's Pythias Sichitalwe pulled out.

body.text: Tonse: cancel it and let us try again

body: The Tonse Alliance, to which the FDD belongs, does not accept the outcome. Its secretary-general, Muhabi Lungu, told News Diggers that the by-election should be cancelled and the alliance allowed to find a new candidate, calling the sudden withdrawals undemocratic and saying the commission should do the right thing. Lungu also said Chisenga had received a telephone call from the Lusaka Province Minister, Obvious Mwaliteta, who allegedly told him he did not want Chisenga to get into trouble. That is Lungu's account; no response from Mwaliteta appeared in the report, and the regulations the commission cited make no provision for a party to substitute a candidate after a withdrawal. Whether the commission has answered Tonse's request is not reported.

The government's reading of the episode came from the Vice-President. During Friday's Vice-President's Question Time, News Diggers and the Zambian Observer reported, Mutale Nalumango said the opposition had to be strong and disciplined and should not expect the ruling party to create political space for it. If opposition parties kept entering contests only to withdraw, she said, the UPND could comfortably declare itself the winner of the 2031 general election; a wrestler who runs before the bout starts, she suggested, is not ready to fight. The Observer's report says she questioned why anyone would file nominations and then pull out.

An unexpected voice agreed with her. Harry Kalaba, the Citizens First leader, said in a statement reported by Daily Revelation and carried by the Zambian Observer that the opposition in its present form should forget about forming government in 2031, that there were "too many chancers within the opposition", and that conduct before and after the 13 August election showed personal gain and political ambition taking priority over ordinary Zambians. The Observer also published a column arguing that Kalaba should be questioning what it called the normalisation of intimidation rather than echoing the Vice-President. On Thursday 5 November, meanwhile, the commission's notice says Banda becomes the member for Mandevu.

body.title: How Mandevu was decided
items: 28 October — withdrawal letters dated by Chisenga (FDD), Mutungwa (Leadership Movement) and Daka (independent)
29 October — letters received by the ECZ, with immediate effect, per the Times of Zambia
30 October — ECZ public notice: Banda the only validly nominated candidate, to be declared elected
5 November — the date the poll had been set for; the declaration takes effect
Also unopposed: Lumezi North (UPND's Anderson Banda) and the Mbala mayoralty (UPND's Felix Mulwanda), per the Times of Zambia

Tonse's call for cancellation is reported by News Diggers. The Vice-President's remarks are reported by News Diggers and the Zambian Observer; Kalaba's statement by Daily Revelation via the Zambian Observer.
body.unverified: Why the three candidates withdrew is not stated in the ECZ notice. Muhabi Lungu's account of a telephone call from Obvious Mwaliteta is an allegation; no response from the minister appeared in the reporting read for this story. Whether the ECZ will respond to Tonse's request is unknown.

stories.title: Fertiliser, irrigation and 10,000 megawatts: in Moscow, Haimbe reads Hichilema's pitch to Russian investors and asks for help with climate preparedness and African-language AI
stories.excerpt: President Hichilema did not travel to the Third Russia-Africa Summit, but his speech did. Delivered at the plenary by Foreign Affairs Minister Mulambo Haimbe, it offered Russian capital a place in fertiliser production, irrigation technology and the power build-out under the Grow Zambia Agenda, repeated the targets of three million tonnes of copper and ten million tonnes of maize, and asked for cooperation on climate adaptation, artificial intelligence and reform of the UN Security Council.

image.label: Zambia's case in Moscow
image.caption: Foreign Affairs Minister Mulambo Haimbe delivered President Hichilema's statement to the plenary of the Third Russia-Africa Summit in Moscow, held on 28 and 29 October 2026.

body: Zambia went to Moscow with a shopping list and a growth target. At the plenary session of the Third Russia-Africa Summit, held on 28 and 29 October, the Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, Mulambo Haimbe, delivered a statement on behalf of President Hakainde Hichilema that invited Russian investors into three areas: fertiliser production, irrigation technology and energy, where the government's stated ambition is 10,000 megawatts of generation. The Times of Zambia and Zambia Monitor both reported the speech; the Times said the approach was framed as one of openness, mutual respect and mutually beneficial economic cooperation.

The frame around the offer was the Grow Zambia Agenda, which aims to double the size of the economy within five years. The Times of Zambia listed the agricultural targets attached to it: ten million tonnes of maize, three million tonnes of soya beans, a million tonnes of wheat and a million tonnes of sugar, with Zambia presenting itself as a regional food basket on the strength of what the speech put at about 40 per cent of southern Africa's water resources. Zambia Monitor added the mining side: a target of three million tonnes of copper a year and a search for partners to process cobalt, manganese and lithium at home rather than export them raw. Haimbe named the Lobito, Nacala and Walvis Bay corridors as the routes that would carry the trade, and the African Continental Free Trade Area as its market.

body.text: Africa's food and energy security are essential to drive healthy and productive human resources and industries.
body.attribution: Mulambo Haimbe, Minister of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation, delivering President Hichilema's statement to the summit plenary in Moscow, as quoted by Zambia Monitor

body.text: Climate, AI and the Security Council

body: The speech also carried requests that were not about capital. According to Zambia Monitor, it noted that Zambia contributes less than 0.01 per cent of global emissions yet saw more than nine million people affected by the 2023/24 drought, and it asked for investment in climate preparedness and anticipatory action. It raised cooperation on artificial intelligence, including technology transfer, digital infrastructure, skills and AI systems for African languages, and it repeated the continent's call for reform of the global financial architecture and of the United Nations Security Council.

Why the minister and not the President went is not explained in the reporting. In a statement on 27 October, the ministry's principal public relations officer, Eva Hatontola Chanda, said Haimbe would deliver Zambia's statement on the President's behalf, attend the Russia-Africa Economic and Humanitarian Forum and meetings on trade, security and technology, and hold engagements on the welfare of Zambians living in Russia; the ministry said Zambia would use the summit to advocate for the peaceful resolution of conflicts and to contribute to discussions on equitable economic partnerships. Hichilema was in Lusaka that week completing his Cabinet. Neither the Times nor Zambia Monitor reported any agreement signed by Zambia in Moscow, and the summit's closing declaration was not covered in the reports read for this story.

stories.title: 12,637 cases in ninety days: police record a rise in gender-based violence for the third quarter, with 2,751 child victims, 49 murders and Lusaka and Luapula top of the table
stories.excerpt: The Zambia Police Service's quarterly statement, issued on Friday 30 October by spokesperson Chipo Kaitisha, counts 7,972 criminal and 4,665 non-criminal GBV cases between July and September. Women and girls were 80.5 per cent of victims. Child victims rose by 433 on the same quarter of 2025 and murders from 30 to 49. The total is also up on the 10,881 cases the police recorded for April to June.

image.label: Q3 2026: 12,637 cases
image.caption: Zambia Police Service figures for July to September 2026 record 12,637 gender-based violence cases, 7,972 of them criminal, with Lusaka Province reporting the most.

body: The police count for the third quarter is higher than the second, and higher than a year ago. In a statement issued in Lusaka on Friday 30 October, the Zambia Police Service spokesperson, Chipo Kaitisha, said 12,637 gender-based violence cases were recorded countrywide between 1 July and 30 September 2026: 7,972 criminal cases and 4,665 non-criminal ones. Zambia Monitor and News Diggers both reported the statement. For April to June, News Diggers reported in September, the police had recorded 10,881 cases, 7,261 of them criminal, so the quarter's total is about 1,750 higher.

Lusaka Province recorded the most criminal cases, 1,610, or about a fifth of the total, followed by Luapula with 1,179 and the Copperbelt with 984, according to Zambia Monitor's account of the provincial table. Western Province had 799, Eastern 707, the Airport Division 692, Southern 629, Central 512, North-Western 436, Northern 238 and Muchinga 137; the TAZARA Division, with 49, was lowest.

Women and girls accounted for 10,167 cases, or 80.5 per cent, and men and boys for 2,470. Children were victims in 2,751 cases, 21.8 per cent of the total and 433 more than the 2,318 recorded in the same quarter of 2025; 2,156 of the child victims were in criminal cases, 1,656 girls and 500 boys. Physical abuse was the largest category, with 4,154 cases, 3,534 of them assault occasioning actual bodily harm, and women were 85.4 per cent of those victims. Economic abuse, mostly the failure to provide necessities of life, accounted for 2,350 cases. Sexual abuse accounted for 957, of which 648 were child defilement, with Lusaka recording 152 of those and Southern Province 100; the police also listed 104 rapes, 21 attempted rapes, 71 indecent assaults and 14 cases of incest. There were 500 cases of emotional and psychological abuse and six of human trafficking.

Forty-nine of the cases were murders, up from 30 in the same quarter last year, involving 24 women, nine men, 11 boys and five girls. The Victim Support Unit counselled 8,914 people over the quarter, 5,043 in criminal matters and 3,871 in non-criminal ones. Kaitisha said the service would strengthen investigations, community sensitisation, child protection and work with other agencies, and called for stronger prevention and response measures. The statement, as reported, did not give the overall total for the third quarter of 2025, only the increases in child victims and murders.

body.text: Women and girls remain disproportionately affected by GBV, accounting for 10,167 cases representing 80.5 percent.
body.attribution: Chipo Kaitisha, Zambia Police Service spokesperson, in a statement issued in Lusaka on Friday 30 October, as quoted by Zambia Monitor

stories.title: 'Not a registered entity': the Chitimukulu asks the Constitutional Court to throw out the petition to make Chief Mukuni a paramount chief, saying the committee behind it cannot sue
stories.excerpt: Paramount Chief Chitimukulu Henry Kanyanta Sosala has filed a summons to dismiss the petition brought in June by the Bene Mukuni Royal Dynasty Committee through its director-general, Jonas Shakafuswa, for want of capacity and jurisdiction. His affidavit says searches at PACRA and the registrars of societies and NGOs on 16 October found no such registered body, and that only the holder of a chief's office can sue over its status.

image.label: The paramountcy petition
image.caption: The Chitimukulu has asked the Constitutional Court to dismiss the petition filed on 25 June 2026 seeking recognition of Chief Mukuni of Kazungula as a paramount chief.

body: The fight over whether Chief Mukuni of Kazungula should be recognised as a paramount chief has reached the question that comes before all the others: whether the people who brought the case can bring it. News Diggers reported on Saturday 31 October, and the Zambian Observer on Thursday 30 October, that Paramount Chief Chitimukulu has asked the Constitutional Court to dismiss the petition filed on 25 June 2026 by the Bene Mukuni Royal Dynasty Committee, acting through its director-general, the former MP Jonas Shakafuswa, against the Attorney-General.

According to the Observer's report by Nelson Zulu, the Chitimukulu, Henry Kanyanta Sosala, filed a summons to dismiss for want of capacity and jurisdiction, supported by an affidavit. The affidavit says searches made on 16 October 2026 at the Patents and Companies Registration Agency, the Registrar of Societies and the Registrar of Non-Governmental Organisations found that the committee is not a registered entity or organisation in Zambia, and that Shakafuswa therefore lacks the legal capacity to commence proceedings on Chief Mukuni's behalf. It argues that the Constitution, as amended in 2016, gives the office of chief perpetual succession and the capacity to sue and be sued in its own name, so that any action about a chief's status must be brought directly by or against the holder of that office, and that recognising or installing a chief is the preserve of the people of the culture concerned. News Diggers' account matches on the central point: the committee, in the Chitimukulu's submission, has no legal capacity to bring the case.

body.text: How the three paramount chiefs got into the case

body: The Chitimukulu, the Litunga of Barotseland and Kalonga Gawa Undi of the Chewa sought to join the petition as interested parties soon after it was filed. News Diggers reported on 23 September that a single judge of the Constitutional Court had dismissed their application and that the three had appealed to the full bench. The Observer's report of 31 October says the court has joined them; the ruling that did so was not among the reports read for this story, and the hearing date for the Chitimukulu's summons is not reported either.

What the petition seeks, in the words of News Diggers' earlier report, is recognition of Chief Mukuni as a paramount chief and a declaration about his current classification; the full text of the relief sought is behind the paper's paywall. No response from Shakafuswa or Chief Mukuni to the application to dismiss appeared in the reporting. A second Observer piece published on Saturday, which describes the committee as illegal and questions Chief Mukuni's lineage, is an opinion article and is not relied on here.

body.confirmed: That the petition was filed on 25 June 2026 by the Bene Mukuni Royal Dynasty Committee through Jonas Shakafuswa against the Attorney-General, and that the Chitimukulu has asked the court to dismiss it for lack of capacity, is reported by News Diggers and the Zambian Observer. The registry searches of 16 October and the constitutional argument are from the Observer's account of the affidavit.
body.unverified: Whether the three paramount chiefs have formally been joined to the case after the September ruling against them is unclear from the reporting. No hearing date is reported. The petitioners' answer to the summons, and the full relief sought, were not available.

stories.title: Africa's first oral cholera vaccine plant breaks ground in November, the President says, as the outbreak that prompted a 709,000-dose campaign stands at 1,622 cases and 30 deaths
stories.excerpt: The Zambia Daily Mail reported on Friday 30 October that President Hichilema, speaking as he swore in his last two ministers, said construction of the vaccine plant at the Lusaka South Multi-Facility Economic Zone would start next month, with a planned 20 million doses a year. The project dates from a 2024 memorandum with a Chinese manufacturer. The Health Minister's latest figures put the outbreak at 1,622 cases in 20 districts since 28 July.

image.label: A plant for the next outbreak
image.caption: The Zambia Daily Mail reported on 30 October 2026 that President Hichilema said construction of an oral cholera vaccine plant at the Lusaka South Multi-Facility Economic Zone would begin in November.

body: In the middle of a cholera outbreak that has needed imported vaccine, the President has set a date for making it at home. The Zambia Daily Mail reported on Friday 30 October that Hakainde Hichilema, speaking as he swore in Christopher Kalila as Minister of Housing and Charles Milupi as Minister of Transport and Logistics, said construction of what he described as Africa's first oral cholera vaccine manufacturing plant would begin next month at the Lusaka South Multi-Facility Economic Zone. The paper said the plant is expected to produce 20 million doses a year and that Hichilema, who is the African Union's cholera champion, called it part of Zambia's contribution to the continental goal of eliminating cholera by 2030.

body.text: We are proud as a nation.
body.attribution: President Hakainde Hichilema, speaking at the swearing-in of ministers Christopher Kalila and Charles Milupi, as quoted by the Zambia Daily Mail on Friday 30 October

body: The project is not new. Anadolu Agency reported on 8 October 2024 that Zambia and China had signed a memorandum of understanding at State House the day before for the country's first cholera vaccine plant, a joint venture between the Industrial Development Corporation and Jijia International Medical Technology Corporation, with a first phase costed at US$37 million and output then expected at about three million doses, and with China to donate about three million doses before production began. Hichilema said at the time that Zambia should be seen as a location to manufacture for a bigger market. The 20 million doses a year the Daily Mail now reports is a different figure from the 2024 one; the reports read for this story do not explain the change.

body.text: The outbreak the plant is too late for

body: The vaccine for the present outbreak came from abroad. Health Minister Roma Chilengi told Parliament this week, as reported by Zambia Monitor and the Daily Mail, that 1,622 cases and 30 deaths had been recorded in 20 districts of six provinces since 28 July, with 228 cases laboratory-confirmed; 16 of the dead died in their communities before reaching a health facility. Of the cases, 1,488 had recovered and been discharged and 104 were still admitted as of 28 October, and the most recent 24-hour period had brought 74 new cases in 12 districts and no deaths. Lusaka Province accounts for 1,090 cases, Central for 298, Luapula for 133, Northern for 88, Southern for 11 and the Copperbelt for two. The International Coordinating Group released 782,147 doses of oral cholera vaccine, and 709,018 people aged a year and over had been vaccinated, 91 per cent of the target, most of them in ten wards of Lusaka District, four in Chibombo and one in Chongwe.

The Treasury has released K13 million to the Ministry of Water Development and Sanitation for emergency safe water supply, and Chilengi said the responsible institutions had to make sure the money turned promptly into safe water for affected and high-risk communities. Hichilema, the Daily Mail reported, said hygiene had to be maintained alongside vaccination and that the government would keep investing in measures against cholera and other public health threats. The plant's start date, the 20-million-dose capacity and the economic-zone site rest on the Daily Mail's report of the President's remarks; no separate statement from the Industrial Development Corporation or the Chinese partner appeared in the reporting read for this story.

stories.title: Champions of Tier B: Zambia's under-15s beat Portugal 5–2 in Baku, Maxen Msimuko scores a hat-trick in the final, and Keith Mweemba tells the squad FAZ will manage what comes next
stories.excerpt: The first FIFA U-15 World Cup ended for Zambia with a trophy on Friday 30 October. Brian Kunsanama's side, placed in Tier B after finishing second in their group, beat England, Niger, Slovakia and Senegal on the way to the final and then Portugal 5–2, with Msimuko's three goals taking him to 16 for the tournament by ZamFoot's count. The result places Zambia 33rd of 189 teams overall.

image.label: Tier B champions, Baku
image.caption: Zambia's under-15s beat Portugal 5–2 in the Tier B final of the inaugural FIFA U-15 World Cup in Baku, Azerbaijan, on Friday 30 October 2026.

body: The week that began with a win over England ended with a trophy. On Friday 30 October, in Baku, Zambia's under-15s beat Portugal 5–2 in the final of Tier B of the inaugural FIFA U-15 World Cup, ZamFoot, News Diggers and Africa Soccer all reported. Maxen Msimuko scored a hat-trick, with further goals from players ZamFoot names only as Benson and Thomson, and Samuel Musonda hit the crossbar. Africa Soccer put the result in the tournament's terms: the Tier B title ranks Zambia 33rd overall in a field of 189 national teams.

The route was long. News Diggers' account of the tournament lists a 13–0 group win over Montserrat and a 2–0 win over Niger, with results against Comoros, England and Slovakia that the paper gives as 2–3, 2–3 and 3–1 without saying which side each figure belongs to. ZamFoot's reports fill in the knockout path: having finished second in their group, which placed them in Tier B rather than Tier A, Zambia beat England in the round of 32, Niger in the round of 16 and Slovakia 3–1 in the quarter-final, and beat Senegal 4–3 in a semi-final in which Moses Munkombwe equalised, Msimuko scored twice and Musonda struck the winner from a Msimuko rebound. Before the final ZamFoot had Msimuko on 13 goals; the hat-trick makes 16.

FIFA's first under-15 World Cup and festival, ZamFoot noted, drew almost 3,000 players from 189 teams across all six confederations, who played 932 matches and scored 4,505 goals, an average of 4.83 a game. Group winners went into Tier A and runners-up into Tier B. Other African teams reaching finals were the Central African Republic, Ethiopia and Tunisia. News Diggers reported that the FAZ president, Keith Mweemba, addressed the squad after the title and gave an assurance about the players' transition to the next age group; the detail of what he promised is behind the paper's paywall, and the coach, Brian Kunsanama, is named by ZamFoot in its semi-final report.

For Zambian football the result sits beside the senior and under-23 teams' November fixtures at a National Heroes Stadium that CAF has approved on a temporary basis, and beside a transitional league in which the Nkana sanction reported elsewhere in this edition was handed down on the same day the under-15s lifted their trophy. The squad's return date was not reported.

Semi-final — beat Senegal 4–3 (Munkombwe, Msimuko 2, Musonda)

stories.title: Two from two at NASDEC: Munali Suns beat Bravehearts and come from ten down against Beira, and meet Botswana's Dolphins on Sunday afternoon with a place in the Elite 16 the prize
stories.excerpt: Zambia's champions opened the Road to BAL 2027 group in Lusaka with a 79–66 win over Malawi's Bravehearts on Friday and an 87–85 recovery against Ferroviario da Beira on Saturday, Douglas Kandulu posting 21 points, 13 rebounds and five blocks. They and the Dolphins are the only unbeaten sides in Group E; the top two go to the East Division Elite 16 in Nairobi from 23 November.

image.label: Munali Suns 2–0
image.caption: Munali Suns beat Bravehearts 79–66 and Ferroviario da Beira 87–85 at the NASDEC Sports Complex in Lusaka in the Road to BAL 2027 Group E, which runs to Tuesday 3 November.

body: Lusaka is hosting one of the five qualifying groups on the road to the Basketball Africa League, and the home side has made the most of it. Munali Suns beat Bravehearts of Malawi 79–66 at the NASDEC Sports Complex on Friday 30 October, News Diggers and FIBA reported, and on Saturday came from ten points down at half-time to beat Mozambique's Ferroviario da Beira 87–85. That leaves the Suns and the Dolphins of Botswana as the only teams with two wins from two in Group E of the Road to BAL 2027, and they play each other at 16:00 on Sunday 1 November.

Friday's win was built on the perimeter and a late run. FIBA's match report credits Ofure Ujadughele with a game-high 26 points, 15 of them in the third quarter, Elijah Mukelabai with 25 points and 13 rebounds and two dunks, and Douglas Kandulu with the rebounds and the blocks; with the score 64–61 and under eight minutes left, Munali scored 12 unanswered points to close it out, while Bravehearts made 10 of 31 three-point attempts. News Diggers, which had Munali 40–31 up at half-time, reported that coach David Musonda afterwards wanted better rebounding and ball retention.

Beira led 43–33 at the interval on Saturday. Mukelabai, who finished with 17 points, eight rebounds and four steals and went six of seven from the free-throw line, brought the deficit to five with a coast-to-coast dunk, and Munali's defence on the three-point line in the second half, FIBA wrote, was the difference. Kandulu had 21 points, 13 rebounds and five blocks, Ujadughele 13 points, five assists and five rebounds; for Beira, Joshua Thomas scored 27 and Ke Tarrious Bouchum 18. In the other Saturday game the Dolphins beat Bravehearts 78–74 after trailing 42–32 at half-time, Dallan Coleman scoring 20, for their second win of the week after beating Harare Kings 77–72 on Friday.

The format rewards the next two days. FIBA's guide to the competition says the top two teams in each of the five groups advance to an Elite 16 round, with the East Division's to be played in Nairobi from 23 to 29 November and the top two there qualifying for the 2027 BAL season. Group E has six teams, the others being Harare Kings of Zimbabwe and South Africa's Soweto Panthers, and FIBA's schedule has the Suns playing the Dolphins on Sunday, the Kings on Monday 2 November and the Panthers on Tuesday 3 November, all at 16:00. FIBA's preview had given the group's dates as 27 to 31 October; the published schedule now runs to 3 November.

stories.title: A K100,000 fine and a ban held in reserve: FAZ's disciplinary committee punishes Nkana for the political chants of 10 October but suspends the five-match exile from Kitwe
stories.excerpt: Three weeks after a section of the crowd at Nkana Stadium sang the campaign song of the detained opposition figures during the 4–1 win over Makeni All Stars, the Football Association of Zambia has ruled. Nkana are fined K100,000 and ordered to play five home games behind closed doors at least 300 km away, but the committee suspended the ban in view of the club's remorse. Nkana say they respect the decision and have asked their supporters to stop.

image.label: Nkana: fined, ban suspended
image.caption: The FAZ Disciplinary Committee's ruling of 30 October 2026 fined Nkana K100,000 over political chanting at the 10 October match against Makeni All Stars and suspended a five-match home ban.

body: The warning of 11 October has become a sanction. ZamFoot reported on Saturday 31 October that the Football Association of Zambia's Disciplinary Committee, ruling on Friday 30 October, found Nkana guilty over the conduct of supporters at the MTN Super League match against Makeni All Stars at Nkana Stadium on 10 October, when some fans were reported to have chanted political slogans. The Zambia Premier League lodged the complaint. The club was first asked to show cause why it should not be disciplined, and answered with an expression of regret and a list of measures to prevent a repeat.

The penalty has two parts. Nkana are fined K100,000. They were also ordered to play their next five home matches at a neutral venue at least 300 kilometres from Nkana Stadium, without spectators; the committee then suspended that ban, citing the club's remorse and its proposed corrective measures, so that Nkana can demonstrate improved supporter conduct for the rest of the season. ZamFoot's report does not say what would trigger the ban's activation beyond a further breach, nor how long the suspension runs beyond the season.

In a statement signed by its media and communications manager, Mike Mubanga, and issued on Saturday, Nkana said it respected the committee's decision and would comply with its directives while working with the football authorities to prevent a recurrence. It spelled out what the suspended ban would cost if it were ever applied: significant financial, logistical and sporting losses, and a stadium closed to the supporters themselves. It asked fans to show restraint, follow football regulations and avoid chants or behaviour that could bring further sanctions.

body.text: Protecting the reputation and future of our beloved club is a collective responsibility.
body.attribution: Nkana FC statement signed by Mike Mubanga, media and communications manager, on Saturday 31 October, as quoted by ZamFoot

body: The ruling closes a loop that opened the day after the match. On Sunday 11 October the Ministry of Youth, Sport and Arts, through its permanent secretary Kangwa Chileshe, condemned political activity at sports venues and asked FAZ, the Zambia Premier League and the clubs to act; News Diggers reported on 12 October that the ministry's statement cited both the Nkana match and Zambia's qualifier against Togo in Ndola, where similar chanting had been observed. FAZ at the time cited CAF and FIFA rules on political neutrality in stadiums but named no sanction. The chant in question, as Lusaka Brief reported on 12 October from Lusaka Times, Zambia Monitor and Zambian Eye, was the campaign song of Brian Mundubile and Makebi Zulu, who remain in custody on treason and terrorism charges with their bail application due back in the High Court on 5 November. The disciplinary ruling, as reported, does not name the song or any individual, and no action against the Togo-match chanting has been reported.

stories.title: A debate at Kaunda's old house earns two Lusaka schools a trip to Uganda, and the heritage commission says it turned a complaint about motorbikes into an exchange programme
stories.excerpt: Learners from Kamwala Secondary and Libala Stage 3 Secondary who debated at Chilenje House during the Independence celebrations have been offered an educational exchange in Uganda by the visiting Afrika Mashariki Fest Group, Zambia Monitor reports. The National Heritage Conservation Commission's Kagosi Mwamulowe said the offer showed what a monument could do beyond standing still.

image.label: Chilenje House, 62 years on
image.caption: Learners from two Lusaka secondary schools who debated at Chilenje House National Monument during the 62nd Independence celebrations have been offered an exchange visit to Uganda.

body: Chilenje House, the small home in Lusaka's Chilenje township where Kenneth Kaunda lived in the years before Independence, is a national monument that most people pass without a second look. During this year's 62nd Independence celebrations it hosted a schools debate, and Zambia Monitor reported on Saturday 31 October that the debate has had an unexpected result: learners from Kamwala Secondary School and Libala Stage 3 Secondary School have been offered an educational exchange programme in Uganda by a visiting Ugandan delegation that watched them argue.

The offer came from the Afrika Mashariki Fest Group, whose chief executive, Ronex Kisembo Tendo, is also a member of the Uganda Bikers Association, which was in Lusaka for the celebrations. Tendo said the delegation would work with the National Heritage Conservation Commission and the Zambian government to arrange the exchange, that Uganda Airlines' flights to Lusaka made the travel practical, and that the aim was to expose the learners to different experiences, broaden their perspectives and strengthen relations between the two countries by investing in young people's intellectual development. Zambia Monitor's report does not name the learners, give the motion they debated or say how long the exchange would last or who would pay for it.

body.text: Lemons, and what a monument is for

body: The commission's executive director, Kagosi Mwamulowe, was candid about how the visit began. The bikers' motorcycles had raised a concern about noise at the monument, he said, and the commission chose to turn the complaint into an opportunity; if you have a lemon, he said, you make lemonade. The offer, in his account, showed that heritage sites can serve education, cultural exchange and tourism rather than only conservation, and that looking after them should include community participation and sustainable development.

Among the visitors was Jimmy Akena Obote, a son of Uganda's former president Milton Obote, who told the gathering that Africa's founding leaders had laid important foundations with few resources and that their sacrifices and vision should keep inspiring work on education, nutrition and housing. The setting made the point for him: Chilenje House is where the man who became Zambia's first president lived while the country he would lead was still being argued into being. For two schools from a few kilometres away, a debate there has become a ticket north.
The exchange's dates, the number of learners involved and the arrangements with the Ministry of Education were not reported. Zambia Monitor's account is, so far, the only report of the offer.

analysis.title: Why diesel rose when oil fell, and what 1 December adds
analysis.body: The November review is small next to October's, but it carries two signals. The first is in the diesel line. The board's own benchmark price for diesel fell by about US$6 a barrel over the review period, yet the pump price went up by K1.18. The only other variable the board named was the kwacha, which it said lost more than 3 per cent. When a currency move alone can lift the price of the fuel that moves maize, cement and buses, the exchange rate becomes the monthly fuel policy whether anyone intends it or not. The second signal is a date. The ERB's October statement recorded that the zero-rating of VAT on fuel ends on 1 December. Unless the government extends it, the December review will have to price in a tax change as well as oil and the kwacha, and October showed what a tax change looks like at the pump. The Vice-President's answer on Friday was that reserves are not for this and the budget is; the 2027 budget is due on 6 November. What to watch is whether it says anything about the VAT date, and whether the kwacha's slide continues into the next review period.

analysis.title: What a walkover settles, and what it leaves open
analysis.body: Mandevu will have a member of Parliament on Thursday without a single vote being counted, and the regulations the commission cited give it no choice: with one validly nominated candidate, there is nothing to poll. That is the settled part. The rest is contested, and each side's case should be stated at its strongest. The government's position, in the Vice-President's words, is that nobody forced three candidates to withdraw after nominating, that a party which retreats from a contest cannot blame its opponent for the result, and that discipline is the opposition's problem to solve. The opposition's position, in Tonse's request and in the allegations that preceded the withdrawals, is that a contest from which candidates say they were frightened out is not a contest, and that an unopposed return reached that way says little about Mandevu's preferences. What is missing is the material that would let a reader decide: the commission's notice gives no reasons for the withdrawals, says nothing about complaints, and no investigation of the alleged threats has been reported. Harry Kalaba's intervention shows the argument is now inside the opposition as well as between it and the UPND. Watch whether the commission answers Tonse, and whether any of the three withdrawn candidates says more.

analysis.title: A suspended ban is a rule with a trigger, and the trigger is the crowd
analysis.body: FAZ has done something more consequential than fine a club. By ordering five closed-door matches 300 kilometres from Kitwe and then suspending them, the disciplinary committee has given Nkana a sanction that its supporters, not its officials, control. The club understood this immediately: its statement is addressed to the stands. The precedent reaches beyond Nkana. The ruling establishes that a chant can cost a Zambian club six figures and its home ground, and it does so without naming the chant, which leaves the next committee to decide what counts as political. Supporters of every club will now be reading that line. There is a fairness question that the reporting has not answered: the same ministry statement that cited Nkana also cited the Zambia–Togo qualifier in Ndola, and no sanction over that match has been reported, so the rule has so far been applied to a club and not to a national-team crowd. What to watch is Nkana's next home fixture, whether the chant travels to other grounds, and whether FAZ publishes the ruling in full so that clubs know where the line is before they cross it.
